title: Scale agents securely with IAM Helper Agent Skills and MCP Tools
summary:
As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blocked even faster as security friction scales.  

To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. 

As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment.

IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance

Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk. 

IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks.

Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). 

Built-in guardrails and real-world impact

Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios:

  • Scaled user-assisted remediation: Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction.

  • Autonomous pipeline self-healing: An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval.

IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously.

  1. Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies: As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor).

  2. Unblocking 403 errors in seconds: When an on-call engineer or deployment agent hits a cryptic 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error, iam-helper-for-troubleshooting identifies the exact missing permission or blocking rule in seconds. It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow).

  3. Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes: Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect.

  4. Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges: When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done.

While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools. 

Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools

Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs). 

Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required.

Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines.

Getting started

Accelerate your agentic workflows, reduce operational overhead, and bring intelligent, scalable security to your deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation.

Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang on Opus 5.5, the Claude Platform, and the engineering behind AI agents. As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. title: claude-code v2.1.312
summary:
What's changed

  • Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub, such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid
  • Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
  • Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
  • Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
  • Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository
  • Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
  • Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output
  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
story_key: story|title:build specialized multimodal models with lfm3
content_excerpt: LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
summary: In a randomized trial, professional analysts working with an AI coding agent went with the option the agent was randomly assigned to favor 86% of the time. We look at what this means for human oversight of AI-assisted work.
story_key: story|title:how ai agents shape experts judgment calls
content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. title: Adaptive Retrieval, Selective Answers: Evaluating Conformal Factuality in Agentic RAG
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve factual grounding without guaranteeing that every generated claim is supported. Previous work has studied claim-level conformal factuality in single-stage RAG and, more recently, multi-hop RAG. We examine its behavior in agentic RAG, where a language-model policy adaptively issues follow-up retrieval queries or terminates retrieval before response generation. We retain the retrieval-based relevance-scoring formulation and post-generation conformal filtering and evaluate six model-dataset configurations: GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B on HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Each configuration uses 60 fixed questions, 100 seeded 30/30 calibration-test partitions, five conformal target levels, and a no-conformal-prediction baseline. Across the six configurations, higher target levels are accompanied by higher observed full-support rates and reduced answer availability. At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage ranges from 17.23% to 60.17%, claim retention from 10.72% to 43.16%, and full support among non-empty outputs from 89.14% to 95.56%. We formulate the adaptive retrieval trajectory explicitly and characterize the reliability-informativeness trade-off when conformal factuality is applied after agent termination.

title: How We Built Our Design Agent
summary: How LangChain built Content Studio, an open-source design agent in Slack that makes on-brand videos, graphics and decks, and the harness that powers it.
story_key: story|title:how we built our design agent
content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing. Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design? The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence” . The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose. Katie Dill , Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison

title: A Unified Arena for LLM Agents across Diverse Eurogame
summary: Interactive environments offer a practical way to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents, and competitive games extend this evaluation to decisions shaped by competing goals and other agents' choices. Yet existing evaluations confined to individual games or execution frameworks leave unclear which competitive advantages persist across settings. We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified arena spanning ten Eurogames with shared interfaces and evaluation protocols. These games combine lasting strategic commitments, competition over shared resources, and multiple routes to victory. Our primary study evaluates 12 model-harness configurations, spanning nine models and four execution harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. The main and supplementary studies comprise 1,032 completed matches in total. These comparisons reveal broad cross-game ranking agreement alongside game-specific strengths. Matched studies show that the same model can perform differently across execution harnesses, adding another source of variation to these profiles. These performance advantages do not consistently translate into better token or cost efficiency, making resource use an additional consideration when comparing configurations. Together, the findings support evaluating complete agent configurations by both their competitive performance across games and the resources needed to achieve it.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
summary: While language models have become dramatically more capable, retrieval still largely relies on lexical matching or similarity in fixed embedding spaces. This creates a capability asymmetry: what the retriever fails to find, even the strongest generator cannot recover. We propose DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of pretrained language models to retrieval using decision models that jointly evaluate candidate branches in a single forward pass, without generating any tokens, and show that judging candidates in a shared context makes their relevance estimates comparable. Like a person browsing a library, DecisionRAG navigates the corpus's inherent structure from broad topics down to individual passages, deciding at each level which branches are worth exploring. Without task-specific training or a first-stage retriever, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Across four benchmarks, including a corpus of 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs, retrieval takes just 0.7-1.8 seconds per query.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.
